title: Tuchel Defends Defensive Tactics After England Collapse Against Argentina
excerpt: England manager Thomas Tuchel blames English football's 'DNA' for the team's inability to hold possession under pressure, insisting his switch to a back five was intended to make the team more active, not more passive.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Tuchel's back five switch aimed to enhance activity, not passivity, amid possession struggles.
  • Argentina surprised by England's defensive substitutions, expecting attacking changes instead.
  • England held just 12% possession after taking the lead against Argentina.
  • FA continues to support Tuchel despite criticism from pundits and former players.
  • Tuchel emphasizes the need for improvement in ball possession for future success.
  • Thomas Tuchel insists his switch to a back five after England took a 1-0 lead was designed to make the team "more active," not more passive, blaming English football's "DNA" for the players' inability to retain possession under pressure.
  • Argentina's players and coaching staff were surprised by Tuchel's defensive substitutions; manager Lionel Scaloni had expected England to introduce pace through Bukayo Saka or Noni Madueke in the second half.
  • Between Anthony Gordon's opening goal and Lautaro Martínez's stoppage-time winner, Argentina held 88% possession to England's 12%.
  • The Football Association continues to back Tuchel, whose contract runs through Euro 2028 on home soil, despite sharp criticism from pundits including Gary Neville.

A Lead Squandered in Atlanta

Anthony Gordon's 55th-minute goal against Argentina in the World Cup semi-final in Atlanta should have been the launch pad for England's first final since 1966. Instead, it became the starting gun for one of the most debated tactical retreats in the nation's football history.

Within 17 minutes of taking the lead, Tuchel replaced goalscorer Gordon with centre-back Ezri Konsa, switching to a back five. Ten minutes later, right-back Reece James and midfielder Declan Rice made way for centre-back Dan Burn and left-back Nico O'Reilly. Seven of England's ten outfield players were now defensive-minded.

Argentina, initially rattled, recalibrated. Enzo Fernández levelled with a fierce long-range strike in the 85th minute. Then, in the second minute of stoppage time, Lionel Messi delivered a cross for Lautaro Martínez to head home the winner. England were out, 2-1.

Tuchel Points to 'DNA' Problem

Speaking in the days after the defeat, Tuchel pushed back against the torrent of criticism, arguing that neither the formation nor the substitutions were the root cause.

"Ball possession plays a crucial role. It's maybe not in our DNA like it is in the Spanish DNA, or the Argentinian-Brazilian DNA, to take the ball and control the game with the ball."

— Thomas Tuchel, England manager

Tuchel said the team's collapse after Gordon's goal was not part of the plan. "Just right after the goal the momentum swings completely and ball possession drops dramatically," he said. "We couldn't find any duels anymore; that's why we dropped deeper and deeper. It was never the plan, but it happened."

He described the back-five switch as an attempt to close gaps inside and win aerial duels against Argentina's increasing number of crosses, not as an invitation to sit deep. "We encourage everyone to step out and to be more active within the structure, but we just struggle," he said.

Tuchel also cited physical fatigue. England covered 14,365 miles during the tournament — more than any other team — and played matches in extreme heat and at altitude, including the group-stage fixture at Mexico City's Azteca Stadium, where they were reduced to ten men.

Argentina Were Stunned

Argentina's camp saw events very differently. According to reporting by The Independent, Scaloni and his coaching staff had identified England's pace in behind as the primary second-half threat and expected Saka or Madueke to come on after the break.

When Tuchel instead loaded defensive substitutions, Scaloni abandoned plans to keep a specialist left-back in reserve. He introduced Martínez for Nicolás Tagliafico in the 81st minute, freeing Nico González to drop back — a move that directly produced the winning goal.

During post-match celebrations, Argentine players discussed their surprise at how quickly England had retreated. The 88-12 possession split from Gordon's goal to the final whistle told the story.

Criticism From Within and Without

England's own players echoed the discomfort. Captain Harry Kane said trying to "hold on" to a 1-0 lead was "not enough at this level." Centre-back Marc Guehi was blunter: "We should have carried on pushing. It kind of felt like we scored and then the mentality was, go back, defend."

Former England defender Gary Neville challenged Tuchel's DNA argument directly, pointing out that Kobbie Mainoo — a starter in the Euro 2024 final and one of the Premier League's most accurate passers in the opposition half — did not play a single minute in the tournament. Phil Foden, Cole Palmer, Adam Wharton, and Trent Alexander-Arnold were all left out of the squad entirely.

"He didn't bring Kobbie Mainoo on, who could handle the ball better than most. He didn't bring Bukayo Saka on. But he also left Phil Foden, Cole Palmer, and Trent Alexander-Arnold at home — technical players, generational talents."

— Gary Neville, Sky Sports

What Comes Next

Despite the outcry, the Football Association continues to back Tuchel. FA Chief Executive Mark Bullingham has privately expressed satisfaction with the German's overall performance, and Sky Sports News reports the FA is not considering his position. Tuchel signed a contract extension in February running through Euro 2028, which England will host.

Tuchel himself insists he remains fully committed. "One hundred per cent," he said. "There is still enough to improve, and I'm more than happy to do that. I still think we can impose ourselves more on the ball."

For England supporters, the question is whether Tuchel can evolve from the manager who shut up shop in Atlanta into one willing to trust his most talented players on the biggest stages. Euro 2028 on home soil — and a nation's patience — will be the test.
